passage:
Friday

Today Ma'am gave back the Hindi test. I got 48 out of 50. Pradeep leaned over to see and I turned it face down fast. He asked, and I said 35. He said, "Good, you're human."
Ever since I won the spelling trophy at assembly, the boys in my row call me Show-off Sid. They bow when I walk past. Pradeep does it too, and he used to share his chips with me.
So now I don't put up my hand even when I know. In maths I knew the answer was 72 and I just sat there. It was a weird feeling, like holding in a sneeze.
Mummy wants to frame the trophy certificate and keeps calling me her clever boy. I told her to keep it in the cupboard.
Sid

qa.q: What mark did Sid actually get in the Hindi test?
qa.a: He got 48 out of 50.

qa.q: How does Sid feel about hiding his answers now?
qa.a: It feels uncomfortable and wrong to him, "like holding in a sneeze", but he does it to stop the teasing.

qa.q: How could a teacher or Mummy support Sid without making the teasing worse?
qa.a: They could praise him privately, keep his results quiet in class, and talk with the class about cheering for each other.

qa.q: What might Pradeep be feeling when he says "Good, you're human"?
qa.a: Pradeep may feel relieved that Sid seems ordinary again, perhaps because the prize made him feel left behind.

grounding: A child mocked as a show-off after winning a prize starts hiding his good marks to fit in.

passage: Yamini found the test paper under the straw in the goat shed, folded into a tight square. Mathematics, 50 out of 50, a star in red ink. She held it up when her brother Ramesh came in with the fodder. "Why is this with the goats?" Ramesh, eleven, grabbed it. "Give it." "You came first in the whole taluka last month. Why hide a test?" He stared at the goat. "On the school bus they call me Collector Saheb. They salute and say 'Show-off, show-off' till we reach the bridge. Yesterday Balu said I think I'm better than the village." "Do you?" "No! I just like numbers." He pushed the paper into his pocket. "If I get sixties now, they'll forget."

qa.a: She found it under the straw in the goat shed, folded into a tight square.

qa.q: Why does Ramesh want to hide his full marks?
qa.a: He is hurt by the teasing on the bus and hopes that if his marks look ordinary, the others will forget and accept him again.

qa.q: What could Yamini do next to help her brother?
qa.a: She could tell their parents or his teacher about the bus teasing and remind Ramesh that liking numbers is nothing to hide.

qa.q: How might Balu see Ramesh's taluka prize?
qa.a: Balu may feel that Ramesh's win makes the other village children look smaller, so mocking him feels like evening things out.

subtype: Downplaying own success to stay liked [Actor]

Monday. The email came during break: Vaibhav had made it to the national quiz finals in Delhi, one of eight from the whole country. Indu read it over his shoulder and squealed. Vaibhav shut the laptop. "They needed someone from the east zone. Pure luck."
Thursday. Mr Fernandes announced it in class. Heads turned. Vaibhav slid down in his seat and said, loud enough, "Don't worry, I'll be out in round one." People laughed. At lunch he skipped the prep session in the library so nobody would see him studying.
The next Tuesday. Walking home, Indu stopped him. "You can actually be happy, you know. Nobody's going to hate you for it." Vaibhav kicked a stone. "They called Rishi 'Mr Topper' for a year." He paused. "I am happy. I'm scared to look it."

I was afraid that if I looked proud, they'd call me big-headed and stop sitting with me. So I went, I painted, I came fourth, and I told nobody. I still have that certificate in a tin. Fourth in India, beta. I wish I had let myself enjoy it for one week.

subtype: Team sniping at the promoted colleague [Observer]
passage:
Thursday night

Three weeks since Nandini moved up to shift supervisor at the front desk, and I'm starting to see what I didn't want to see. Nobody covers her breaks any more. Today she ate standing behind the counter. When the guest in 214 complained about the AC, Rukhsana took the call and "forgot" to pass it on, so Nandini heard about it from me, in front of the guest. At the evening briefing, when she spoke, Anil and two others looked at their phones. Someone has started calling her "Madam Supervisor" in a sing-song voice. Before this they were a gang, all four of them. Birthday cakes, shared autos home.
I promoted her because she was the best. Tomorrow I'll talk to the team, and to her, separately.
Farida

passage: You want the honest version, Vaibhav? Okay. Last March, my junior from B.Ed college, Rukhsar, won the state award for young teachers. Two years younger than me. When I saw the photo, my first thought was: she only won because her school is in the city. I actually typed half of that to a friend. Then I stopped and said it out loud in my empty kitchen: Yamini, you're jealous. Just call it what it is. It felt silly, but it helped. So I deleted the message and called Rukhsar instead. I said congratulations and I meant most of it. Then I asked what she'd done in her classroom that got noticed. She laughed, said "Thank you, Didi," and told me about her reading corner for first-generation learners. And I realised the award didn't sting because of her. It stung because I've wanted to start something like that for three years and haven't.

passage: Every wedding in Kherwadi had the same brass band, and the band had one favourite tune: loud, wobbly trumpets that sounded, Devika thought, like buffaloes arguing. And at the fourth wedding, in Phalgun, when the band struck up by the temple steps, Devika was in the middle of the dancing girls, spinning with her arms up. Last winter my flatmate Jaya asked me, for the fourth time, to come with her to an evening of Marathi stage songs at the old theatre in Dadar. I'd always said no. The singing sounded fussy to me, too many turns in every line. But that week I'd read somewhere that we often like things just because we know them, and it made me wonder about my playlist, which was the same film songs I'd had since school. So I made a deal with myself: three evenings, full attention, then decide. The first night I checked the time a lot. The second, one slow song stuck with me on the train home. By the third, I was waiting for a particular singer. I still don't love all of it. But I love her voice, and I wouldn't know that if I'd trusted my first no.
Uma

qa.q: What did Deepika's approach of three Fridays do well?
qa.a: It gave each dish a fair chance, so her final choices, keeping the stew and passing on the noodles, came from real tasting rather than habit.

qa.q: How might Tesfaye feel when Deepika asks him to save her some stew?
qa.a: He might feel appreciated and welcomed, since his home food has become something a colleague looks forward to.

grounding: A supervisor notes an adult who deliberately gives unfamiliar foods a few fair tries before deciding.
